title: Exploring Magnets
description: Grade 6 Science: magnetic and non-magnetic materials, poles of a magnet, attraction and repulsion, and the magnetic compass — notes, solved examples and a test.

topics.title: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Materials
topics.concept:
A magnet is an object that attracts materials made of iron, and a few other metals, towards it. Magnets were first discovered as a natural rock called magnetite (an ore of iron) found long ago near a place called Magnesia — which is how magnets got their name.

Materials are of two kinds, based on how a magnet affects them:

  • Magnetic materials — those that are attracted by a magnet. Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Most steel objects (steel contains iron) are also attracted.
  • Non-magnetic materials — those that are not attracted by a magnet. Wood, plastic, paper, rubber, cloth, glass, copper and aluminium are non-magnetic.

You can test any object by bringing a magnet close to it: if it is pulled towards the magnet, it is magnetic. This simple property is very useful — for example, in scrapyards a large magnet is used to lift and separate iron objects from a heap of mixed waste, leaving the non-magnetic materials behind.

Magnets are made in different shapes for different uses: a bar magnet, a horseshoe (U-shaped) magnet, a cylindrical magnet and a ring magnet are common ones.

examples.problem: Example 1: From this list, pick the magnetic materials: iron nail, plastic ruler, steel spoon, rubber band, copper wire.
examples.solution:
Magnetic materials are those attracted by a magnet — mainly iron and steel (which contains iron).

  • Iron nail — magnetic.
  • Steel spoon — magnetic (steel contains iron).
  • Plastic ruler, rubber band, copper wire — non-magnetic.
examples.answer: The iron nail and the steel spoon are magnetic; the plastic ruler, rubber band and copper wire are non-magnetic.

examples.problem: Example 2: How is a large electromagnet used to separate iron from a mixed heap of waste at a scrapyard?
examples.solution:
Only magnetic materials are attracted by a magnet.

  • The magnet is brought near the heap.
  • Iron and steel objects are pulled to the magnet and lifted away.
  • Non-magnetic materials (plastic, glass, wood) are left behind.
examples.answer: The magnet attracts and lifts the iron/steel objects, leaving the non-magnetic waste behind, separating the two.

examples.problem: Example 3: A magnet does not stick to a one-rupee coin. What can you conclude about the metal of the coin?
examples.solution:
If a magnet does not attract a metal, that metal is non-magnetic.

  • The coin is not made mainly of iron, nickel or cobalt.
  • It is likely made of a non-magnetic metal such as aluminium or a copper alloy.
examples.answer: The coin is made of a non-magnetic metal (such as aluminium or a copper alloy), not iron.

recap:
• A magnet attracts iron and a few other metals; natural magnet = magnetite.
  • Magnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt, steel) are attracted; non-magnetic materials (wood, plastic, copper, aluminium, glass) are not.
  • Test an object by bringing a magnet near it — attraction means it is magnetic.
  • Common shapes: bar, horseshoe, cylindrical and ring magnets.

quiz.q: Which of these materials is attracted by a magnet?
quiz.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material; the others are non-magnetic.

quiz.q: The natural magnet found as an ore of iron is called:
quiz.explanation: Magnetite is the naturally occurring magnetic ore of iron.

topics.title: Poles of a Magnet
topics.concept:
If you dip a bar magnet into a tray of iron filings and lift it out, you will see that the filings cling mostly at the two ends and very little in the middle. These two ends, where the magnet’s pull is strongest, are called the poles of the magnet.

Every magnet has two poles — a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). The pull of a magnet is strongest at the poles and weakest in the middle.

A remarkable property: when a magnet is hung freely so that it can swing, it always comes to rest pointing in the north–south direction. The end that points towards the Earth’s geographic north is called the north-seeking pole (north pole), and the other is the south-seeking pole (south pole). This is the basis of the compass.

You cannot get a magnet with only one pole. If you break a bar magnet into two pieces, you do not get a separate N piece and a separate S piece — instead, each smaller piece becomes a complete magnet with its own north and south pole.

examples.problem: Example 1: A bar magnet is rolled in iron filings. Why do the filings stick mostly at the two ends?
examples.solution:
The strength of a magnet is not the same everywhere.

  • The pull is strongest at the two ends, called the poles.
  • So more filings cling at the ends and few in the middle.
examples.answer: Because the magnet’s pull is strongest at its poles (the two ends), so the filings gather there.

examples.problem: Example 2: A bar magnet is cut into two equal pieces. How many poles does each piece have?
examples.solution:
A single pole cannot exist on its own.

  • Each broken piece becomes a complete magnet.
  • So each piece has two poles — one north and one south.
examples.answer: Each piece becomes a complete magnet with two poles (one north and one south).

examples.problem: Example 3: A freely suspended bar magnet always settles pointing north–south. What is the name of the end that points towards the north?
examples.solution:
The poles are named by the direction they seek.

  • The end pointing to geographic north is the north-seeking pole.
  • This is simply called the north pole (N).
examples.answer: It is the north-seeking pole, i.e. the north pole (N).

recap:
• The poles are the two ends of a magnet where its pull is strongest.
  • Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole; a single pole cannot exist alone.
  • A freely hung magnet rests in the north–south direction.
  • Breaking a magnet gives two smaller magnets, each with both poles.

quiz.q: The pull of a magnet is strongest at its:
quiz.explanation: A magnet’s force is strongest at the two poles.

quiz.q: If a bar magnet is broken into two pieces, each piece will have:
quiz.explanation: Each piece becomes a complete magnet with both poles; a single pole cannot exist.

topics.title: Attraction and Repulsion
topics.concept:
When the poles of two magnets are brought near each other, they either pull together or push apart, depending on which poles face each other. This gives us the basic law of magnetic poles:

  • Like poles repel — two north poles (N–N), or two south poles (S–S), push away from each other.
  • Unlike poles attract — a north pole and a south pole (N–S) pull towards each other.

This pushing and pulling happens even without the magnets touching, because a magnet has an invisible region of influence around it called its magnetic field.

There is an important difference between attraction and repulsion. A magnet attracts a piece of ordinary iron (which is not itself a magnet) and attracts the opposite pole of another magnet. But repulsion happens only between two magnets. So if object A pushes object B away, both A and B must be magnets. This makes repulsion the sure test for finding out whether an object is truly a magnet.

examples.problem: Example 1: The north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another. Will they attract or repel?
examples.solution:
Apply the law of poles.

  • Both are north poles — these are like poles.
  • Like poles repel.
examples.answer: They will repel (push apart), because like poles repel.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is repulsion, and not attraction, the sure test for a magnet?
examples.solution:
Think about what each behaviour means.

  • A magnet attracts both ordinary iron and the opposite pole of another magnet — so attraction alone does not prove the other object is a magnet.
  • Repulsion happens only between two magnets.
  • So if two objects repel, both must be magnets.
examples.answer: Because attraction can occur with ordinary iron too, but repulsion occurs only between two magnets — so repulsion is the sure test.

examples.problem: Example 3: Two objects, P and Q, push each other apart when brought close. What can you say about P and Q?
examples.solution:
Use the sure test for magnets.

  • They repel, and only two magnets can repel.
  • So both P and Q are magnets, with like poles facing each other.
examples.answer: Both P and Q are magnets (like poles were facing each other), since only magnets repel.

recap:
• Like poles repel (N–N, S–S); unlike poles attract (N–S).
  • Magnets act without touching, through their magnetic field.
  • Attraction can occur with ordinary iron, but repulsion happens only between two magnets.
  • Therefore repulsion is the sure test for a magnet.

options: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract
quiz.explanation: Like poles repel each other and unlike poles attract each other.

quiz.q: The sure test to check whether an object is a magnet is:
quiz.explanation: Only two magnets can repel, so repulsion is the sure test for a magnet.

topics.title: The Magnetic Compass
topics.concept:
Because a freely suspended magnet always points north–south, people long ago used magnets to find direction. This led to the invention of the magnetic compass — a small, light, magnetised needle that is balanced on a pivot so it can turn freely inside a case marked with directions.

The compass needle is itself a tiny magnet. When left free, its north pole points towards the Earth’s geographic north, so you can read off all the directions — north, south, east and west. Sailors, travellers and explorers used the compass to find their way long before modern devices existed.

You can even make a temporary magnet by stroking a steel needle many times in the same direction with one pole of a bar magnet. The needle becomes magnetised and, if floated on a piece of cork in water, behaves like a compass.

Magnets must be cared for, because they can lose their magnetism if they are dropped, hammered, heated strongly, or stored carelessly. Bar magnets should be stored in pairs with unlike poles together and a small soft-iron piece (a ‘keeper’) across the ends; a horseshoe magnet is stored with a single keeper across its poles.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why does the needle of a compass always come to rest in a fixed direction?
examples.solution:
The needle is a small, freely turning magnet.

  • A free magnet always settles in the north–south direction.
  • So the needle’s north pole points to the Earth’s north, giving a fixed direction.
examples.answer: Because the needle is a tiny free magnet, and a free magnet always rests pointing north–south.

examples.problem: Example 2: How can you magnetise a steel needle using a bar magnet?
examples.solution:
Stroking transfers magnetism to the steel.

  • Stroke the needle many times with one pole of the bar magnet.
  • Always stroke in the same direction, lifting the magnet away each time.
  • The needle becomes a magnet.
examples.answer: Stroke the needle many times in the same direction with one pole of the magnet; it becomes magnetised.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two ways a magnet can lose its magnetism.
examples.solution:
Rough treatment weakens a magnet.

  • Dropping or hammering it.
  • Heating it strongly (or storing it carelessly).
examples.answer: By dropping/hammering it or by heating it strongly (careless storage also weakens it).

recap:
• A magnetic compass is a freely turning magnetised needle that shows direction.
  • The needle’s north pole points to geographic north.
  • A steel needle can be magnetised by stroking in one direction with a magnet.
  • Magnets lose magnetism if dropped, hammered or heated; store bar magnets in pairs with keepers.

quiz.q: A compass works because its needle is a small magnet that:
quiz.explanation: A free magnet settles north-south, so the compass needle shows direction.

quiz.q: A magnet may lose its magnetism if it is:
quiz.explanation: Heating, dropping or hammering a magnet weakens or destroys its magnetism.

questions.q: A magnet attracts objects made mainly of:
questions.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material attracted by a magnet.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-magnetic material?
questions.explanation: Copper is non-magnetic; iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic.

questions.q: The natural magnet is an ore of iron called:
questions.explanation: Magnetite is the naturally occurring magnetic ore of iron.

questions.q: Every magnet has:
questions.explanation: Every magnet has a north and a south pole.

questions.q: The magnetic pull of a bar magnet is strongest at its:
questions.explanation: The force is strongest at the two poles.

questions.q: When a bar magnet is broken into two, each piece:
options: Becomes a complete magnet with two poles
questions.explanation: A single pole cannot exist; each piece is a full magnet.

questions.q: Two south poles brought near each other will:
questions.explanation: Like poles repel each other.

questions.q: A north pole and a south pole brought close will:
questions.explanation: Unlike poles attract.

questions.q: The sure test to identify a magnet is:
questions.explanation: Only two magnets can repel, so repulsion is the sure test.

questions.q: A freely suspended bar magnet always rests pointing:
questions.explanation: A free magnet aligns north-south, the basis of the compass.

questions.q: The region around a magnet where its force acts is called the:
questions.explanation: The magnetic field is the region of influence around a magnet.

questions.q: A steel needle can be turned into a magnet by:
options: Stroking it in one direction with a magnet
questions.explanation: Stroking in one direction with a magnet magnetises the needle.

questions.q: A device that uses a magnetised needle to show direction is the:
questions.explanation: A magnetic compass shows direction.

questions.q: Which action can make a magnet lose its magnetism?
questions.explanation: Strong heating, dropping or hammering weakens a magnet.

questions.q: At a scrapyard, a large magnet is used to:
options: Separate iron objects from other waste
questions.explanation: The magnet attracts and lifts iron, separating it from non-magnetic waste.

questions.q: Object A attracts object B, but A does not repel B from any side. What can you conclude?
options: Both A and B are definitely magnets
A is a magnet and B may be a magnet or a piece of iron
B is a magnet and A is iron
questions.explanation: Attraction alone is not proof; only repulsion confirms both are magnets.

questions.q: Iron filings are sprinkled on a bar magnet. The pattern shows fewest filings at the middle because there:
questions.explanation: The force is weakest in the middle and strongest at the poles.

questions.q: A magnet is cut into three pieces. The total number of poles among the three pieces is:
questions.explanation: Each piece is a complete magnet with 2 poles, so 3 pieces have 6 poles.

questions.q: Why must a bar magnet not be hammered or dropped repeatedly?
questions.explanation: Rough treatment disturbs the magnet and weakens or destroys its magnetism.

questions.q: A floating magnetised needle on cork points north-south. If you bring the north pole of a bar magnet near its north-seeking end, the needle end will:
questions.explanation: Two north poles are like poles, so they repel and the needle end moves away.

questions.q: Which property of a freely suspended magnet makes the compass possible?
questions.explanation: A free magnet aligns north-south, which lets a compass show direction.
